the-game-loop-time-and-state.title: Welcome to The game loop, time and state, part of Game Development: 2D, 3D, 4D, 5D and 4K–8K+.
the-game-loop-time-and-state.idea: A film is a recording; a game is a conversation. Sixty times a second the machine asks two questions: what is the world now, given what the player just did, and what does that world look like? Everything in this course, from a tile map to a spinning hypercube to an 8K picture, hangs from that rhythm. Two ideas keep returning. The first is that the world has dimensions: two, three, four, five, and as many as you care to define. Those decide what you simulate. The second is that the picture has dimensions too: 1080p, 4K, 8K and beyond. Those decide how much work it takes to show the world. Both are paid for from the same small allowance of time, about 16.7 milliseconds per frame at 60 frames per second. This first lesson is about that allowance and the loop that spends it. Ghana is a good place to learn this the hard way. Many players are on mid-range Android phones that heat up, slow down to protect themselves, and run on a battery between power cuts. A loop that is only correct on a fast laptop is only correct for some of your players.
the-game-loop-time-and-state.example: Run this in the JavaScript console. Part 1 simulates one second at three frame rates, with movement written both ways. Part 2 drops a bouncing ball for six seconds twice, once with steady 16 ms frames and once with irregular frames that add up to exactly the same time. Predict the numbers before you run it.
the-game-loop-time-and-state.challenge: Build the loop for a small game of your own in the web playground: a fixed 60 Hz simulation with an accumulator and a clamp, interpolated drawing, an on-screen readout of frame time and updates per second, and a key that injects a 200 ms stall. Show, with a screenshot or written notes, that the distance an object has travelled after ten seconds is identical at 30 fps, at 60 fps and with random stalls.

worlds-in-2d-sprites-tilemaps-collisions.title: Welcome to 2D worlds: sprites, tile maps, collisions and the camera, part of Game Development: 2D, 3D, 4D, 5D and 4K–8K+.
worlds-in-2d-sprites-tilemaps-collisions.idea: Two dimensions is where most games, and most game developers, begin, and it is also where a surprising number of successful games stay. Celeste, Stardew Valley and Hollow Knight are 2D. So are the mobile games that millions of people play on modest phones. Ghana has its own tradition here: Accra's Leti Arts has published mobile games and comics rooted in African folklore since 2009. The reason is practical. A 2D game can be a few megabytes, needs no 3D art pipeline, runs on a phone that could not hold a 3D game's textures, and its rules fit in your head. It is also the best place to learn the ideas that never go away: grids, collisions, cameras and the discipline of the fixed step from lesson 1.
worlds-in-2d-sprites-tilemaps-collisions.example: This sample is the whole collision system for a tile game in under a hundred lines. The map is four rows of ten tiles, 16 pixels each, with wall tiles in the third row and a floor in the fourth. Work out by hand where each box should end up, then run it.
worlds-in-2d-sprites-tilemaps-collisions.challenge: Extend the demo into a three-screen game: coins that count, a spike tile that sends the player back to the start of the screen, a goal flag that loads a second map from text, and a switch that draws the world at 480 × 270 and scales it by whole numbers. Hand in the map text, a paragraph explaining how your collisions are resolved, and screenshots at two different window sizes with pixels that stay sharp.

worlds-in-3d-vectors-matrices-and-projec.title: Welcome to 3D worlds: vectors, matrices and projection, part of Game Development: 2D, 3D, 4D, 5D and 4K–8K+.
worlds-in-3d-vectors-matrices-and-projec.idea: The step from 2D to 3D looks like adding a z. It is really a change of kind. In 2D you place pictures; in 3D you place objects in a world and the screen becomes a window onto it, so "where does this point land on the screen?" becomes a calculation rather than a position you chose. The good news is that the mathematics is small. Everything in this lesson fits in a few hundred lines, and you will write a working 3D renderer from scratch before the end. The reason to do it once by hand is that every call you will later make in an engine, the camera, lookAt, the projection matrix, the normals, stops being magic.
worlds-in-3d-vectors-matrices-and-projec.example: Each part of this sample answers one question. Which targets can a guard see? Which way does a triangle face? How bright is a surface lit from four directions? Where does one corner of a cube land on a 1920 × 1080 screen, and what happens when it moves away?
worlds-in-3d-vectors-matrices-and-projec.challenge: Extend the cube demo into a small scene: three objects (a cube, a pyramid and a plane) each with its own model transform, a camera that orbits when you drag, back-face culling, and Lambert shading using normals from cross products. Report the vertex and triangle counts and how long a frame takes, measured with performance.now().

building-in-3d-light-physics-and-engines.title: Welcome to Building in 3D: light, physics, performance and engines, part of Game Development: 2D, 3D, 4D, 5D and 4K–8K+.
building-in-3d-light-physics-and-engines.idea: Lesson 3 built a renderer in under a hundred lines of JavaScript. A modern engine is millions of lines, and the question is what you are buying. The answer is a scene editor, importers for models and sound, a physics engine, animation, input, interface tools, and build tools that produce an Android package or a web page. You are paying for time. What you are not buying is judgment. The engine hands you the controls: a normal map, a shadow distance, a draw-call count. It does not tell you which ones matter on a phone with 3 GB of memory. For that you need the ideas in this lesson, and the frame budget from lesson 1.
building-in-3d-light-physics-and-engines.example: Press Run page. Two spheres are lit from a light that orbits them. Their surface normals are never stored: for a sphere, the normal at a point is simply that point divided by the radius, so the code computes nz = sqrt(1 − nx² − ny²) and has everything it needs. The left sphere uses diffuse light only; the right adds the specular highlight. When the light swings behind them, the lit part shrinks to a thin rim, because max(0, N · L) is zero wherever the surface faces away. Drag Shininess and watch the highlight tighten. Then try a change of your own: add a coloured light, add a rim light with pow(1 − N · V, 3), or quantise the diffuse value into three bands to get a cartoon look.
building-in-3d-light-physics-and-engines.challenge: Build a small 3D prototype in the engine or library you chose: a character on a fixed-step capsule controller, a ray-cast ground check, three kinds of light, two LOD levels for one prop and an on-screen frame-time counter. Test it on a mid-range phone or the weakest machine you own, and write half a page on what the bottleneck was and how you proved it by changing the resolution.

the-fourth-dimension-of-space.title: Welcome to The fourth dimension of space, part of Game Development: 2D, 3D, 4D, 5D and 4K–8K+.
the-fourth-dimension-of-space.idea: Four different things get called "4D" in games, and they have little in common except the name. There is a fourth direction of space, at right angles to the three we live in. There is time, treated as a dimension you can store and replay. There is the fourth number that sits in every vertex and every rotation inside a normal 3D engine. And there is 4D entertainment, the cinema seat that tilts and sprays mist. This lesson is about the first. Lesson 6 takes the other three. So for this lesson, "4D" means a fourth spatial direction. Not time. The developers of the 4D games below are firm about it, and so should you be: if you let the two meanings blur, none of the mathematics makes sense. The good news is that the mathematics is not harder than 3D, only longer. If you can write the cube in lesson 3, you can write a tesseract by changing one number.
the-fourth-dimension-of-space.example: Everything above, in about a hundred lines. The sample builds the tesseract from the "differ in one coordinate" rule, checks the counts against the formula, turns it in the xw plane and slices it three ways. Predict how many points each slice will have before you run it.
the-fourth-dimension-of-space.challenge: Build a 4D toy of your own: a tesseract or a small 4D grid of cubes with mouse-driven rotation in at least three planes, a slice view beside the projection view, and a colour scheme that encodes w. Write half a page on what a player can and cannot work out from each of the two views.

the-fourth-dimension-of-time-and-sensati.title: Welcome to The fourth dimension of time and sensation, part of Game Development: 2D, 3D, 4D, 5D and 4K–8K+.
the-fourth-dimension-of-time-and-sensati.idea: Ask ten people what a 4D game is and you will hear at least three answers. Lesson 5 covered a fourth direction of space. This lesson covers the other two. One is time, which games manipulate constantly: pausing, slowing, rewinding, looping. The other is sensation, the cinema-seat sense of 4D, where the world pushes back with motion, wind and mist. Both reduce to the same discipline: treat time as an axis you can index, store and schedule. A game that can say "what was the state at tick 1,800?" can replay, rewind, make ghosts and reproduce bugs. A game that can say "send the fan cue 400 milliseconds before the splash" can build a ride.
the-fourth-dimension-of-time-and-sensati.example: A tiny deterministic game, a thing sliding left and right and bouncing off walls, driven by 3,600 seeded inputs (60 seconds at 60 ticks a second). The sample plays it live and saves a keyframe each second, then replays it from the inputs alone, rewinds to tick 2,500, counts the memory each approach would need for 2,000 moving things, and finally shows what one hidden Math.random() does.
the-fourth-dimension-of-time-and-sensati.challenge: Add a ghost to your game from lesson 2: record the player's inputs for their best run, replay it as a translucent second player at the same time, prove with a fingerprint that two replays match, and add a rewind key limited to the last five seconds using keyframes. Write down your memory budget for history in bytes.

five-dimensions-and-beyond.title: Welcome to Five dimensions and beyond, part of Game Development: 2D, 3D, 4D, 5D and 4K–8K+.
five-dimensions-and-beyond.idea: "Dimension" is the most overloaded word in this course. In lessons 2 to 5 it meant a direction in space. In lesson 6 it meant time. Here we meet the general meaning: a dimension is one independent number you need in order to say where you are in a space of states. By that definition a chessboard square has two (file and rank), and the graphics menu of a game, with its resolution, shadow quality, texture quality and frame cap, is a four-dimensional space that you ask the player to navigate. Once dimension means "independent axis of state", the number five is no longer exotic. It is simply one more axis, and the code you have already written does not care how many there are.
five-dimensions-and-beyond.example: A Multiverse class with one rule: playing on the newest board of a timeline extends it, and playing on an older board forks a new timeline. Boards are frozen, so history cannot be changed even by accident. The sample plays three moves on the original timeline, goes back to turn 1 and plays differently, then goes back again inside the new timeline.
five-dimensions-and-beyond.challenge: Choose a game idea whose state has at least five independent axes, for example grid x, grid y, time, timeline and a power level. Write down its state space and a move generator that takes steps of ±1 along axes, a breadth-first search that proves a puzzle is solvable and reports the shortest solution, and a plan for showing it to a player with linked 2D views. Estimate the memory needed with dense and with sparse storage.

ultra-high-resolution-4k-8k-and-beyond.title: Welcome to Ultra-high resolution: 4K, 8K and beyond, part of Game Development: 2D, 3D, 4D, 5D and 4K–8K+.
ultra-high-resolution-4k-8k-and-beyond.idea: A 4K screen has four times as many pixels as a 1080p one. An 8K screen has sixteen times as many, and 16K has sixty-four times. Every one of those pixels runs your shader sixty times a second. Resolution is the most expensive setting in most games and the one players ask for first, because the number is printed on the box. This lesson is arithmetic. Not because the arithmetic is hard, but because the results are always surprising, and surprising results are cheaper to meet on paper than in the last week of a project. Run the numbers before you promise 8K. A note on names. The "K" in 4K and 8K counts thousands of pixels across, roughly, while the "p" in 1080p counts lines of height. So "4K" and "2160p" are the same thing wearing different labels, and the two systems should not be mixed.
ultra-high-resolution-4k-8k-and-beyond.example: Five questions in one program: how big is each step of the ladder, how long does each pixel get at 60 fps, how much memory do the frame buffers take, how much memory traffic does a frame cause, and what does the picture cost on the cable?
ultra-high-resolution-4k-8k-and-beyond.challenge: Write a one-page resolution policy for a game of your own: the default render resolution for three device classes (a low-end phone, a laptop and a 4K television), the texture sizes and compression for each, the memory budget for frame buffers and textures, and the download size per class, each justified with pixels per degree and the arithmetic from this lesson.

scaling-to-every-screen-and-shipping.title: Welcome to Scaling to every screen, and shipping, part of Game Development: 2D, 3D, 4D, 5D and 4K–8K+.
scaling-to-every-screen-and-shipping.idea: Lesson 8 ended with an uncomfortable answer: you cannot simply shade every pixel of every screen. This lesson is the toolbox for not having to. The ideas fall into three groups. Measure, so you know what is slow. Adapt, changing how many pixels you shade while the game runs. And ship, so the game reaches the player and runs on the device in their hand, not the one on your desk.
scaling-to-every-screen-and-shipping.example: A pretend 4K graphics card, a fixed 2 ms of geometry plus a cost that grows with pixels, and a two-second explosion that makes every pixel almost twice as expensive. The controller uses the square-root rule, falls at up to 10% a frame, rises at 4%, and stays within 50% to 100%.
scaling-to-every-screen-and-shipping.challenge: Deliver the course project, Dimensions: a playable build with a fixed-step loop, a 2D level, a 3D scene, a 4D or 5D toy and a render-scale control with dynamic resolution. Include a two-page report with p50, p95 and p99 frame times at four render scales on two devices, the pixels per degree of your target screen, a CPU-bound or GPU-bound verdict with the experiment that proved it, a quality-tier table and the download size per tier.
